passage:
Paragraph A
For most of the twentieth century the policy of land agencies across North America was simple and, on its own terms, successful: put out every fire as quickly as possible. The reasoning seemed self-evident. Fire destroys timber, threatens property and kills people, and a fire extinguished while small never becomes a fire that cannot be extinguished at all. What the policy did not take into account was that in many landscapes fire is not an interruption of the natural order but part of it.

Paragraph B
A great many wildland areas are what ecologists call fire-adapted or fire-dependent, meaning they require periodic burning to remain healthy and resilient. The evidence is written into the plants themselves. Some pines carry cones sealed with resin that open only when heated, so that seed is released precisely when the ground has been cleared and fertilised by ash. Certain trees develop bark thick enough to insulate the living tissue beneath from a fire moving through the undergrowth. Others are killed above ground but resprout vigorously from roots that the fire never reached. These are not accidents of survival; they are adaptations to an event the plants can rely on.

Paragraph C
When fire is removed from such a system, the material that would have burned does not disappear. Dead branches, needles, leaf litter and thickets of young stems accumulate each year that no fire comes, and the forest grows denser and more continuous than it historically was. Foresters call this accumulated material fuel, and its quantity and arrangement determine not whether a fire will eventually occur but how it will behave when it does. A landscape that once burned lightly every few years may, after decades of protection, be capable of carrying a fire into the canopy that nothing can stop.

Paragraph D
The response has been to reintroduce fire deliberately. A prescribed fire is a planned fire, sometimes called a controlled burn, lit to meet stated management objectives: reducing hazardous fuels, restoring fire to vegetation types that depend on it, creating diverse habitat, assisting the recovery of endangered species, and maintaining historic landscapes. The word prescribed is used in something close to its medical sense — a treatment specified in advance for a particular condition.

Paragraph E
The specification is literal. Before any burning takes place a park must complete a fire management plan and, for the individual operation, a burn plan. The scientific prescription prepared in advance describes the objectives, the fuels, the size of the burn, the precise environmental conditions under which it will be allowed to burn, and the conditions under which it must instead be suppressed. A prescription in this sense is a set of conditions weighing the safety of the public and of the fire staff, the weather, and the probability that the objectives will actually be met.

Paragraph F
On the day, none of this is assumed. Every prescribed fire must satisfy all the conditions identified on a go/no-go checklist before a single flame is lit, and if any of them falls outside the prescription the operation is postponed, however inconvenient the delay. Ignition itself is a matter of technique rather than chance. Crews on foot use drip torches to lay lines of fire in a chosen pattern; flare guns extend that reach; and where terrain is inaccessible a helicopter can dispense plastic spheres containing potassium permanganate, injected with glycol so that each ignites a short time after it lands.

Paragraph G
The results are measurable, and they persist. Areas treated by prescribed burning have repeatedly been observed to change the behaviour of later wildfires, slowing their advance and dropping them out of the canopy where the previously treated ground is reached. Repeated treatment matters more than any single burn, because what managers are trying to rebuild is not a cleared area but a mosaic — a patchwork of stands of different ages and fuel loads across the landscape, which is what limited the size of fires before suppression began.

Paragraph H
None of this makes prescribed burning easy to carry out. The prescription windows are narrow, smoke drifts into communities that did not ask for it, and an escaped burn is a career-ending event for those responsible, whereas a fire that was never lit costs nobody anything visible. The incentives, in other words, point the wrong way. That is the central difficulty of the policy: its benefits are diffuse, delayed and statistical, while its risks are immediate, local and attributable.

(Glossary: fuel: material such as dead wood, litter and small stems that a fire can burn; canopy: the upper layer of foliage in a forest; resprout: to grow new shoots after the above-ground parts have been destroyed; drip torch: a hand-held canister that drips burning fuel to start a line of fire.)
